entry.evidence: It has long been hypothesized that topographic upwelling is responsible for such characteristics

steps.action: Mapped MODIS entire-mission SST and chlorophyll-a composites showing cool, productive pools immediately west of the Gilbert and Galápagos Islands (Figure 1).
steps.quote: Found immediately west of the Gilbert and Galápagos Islands are localized enhancements of the surface characteristics of the cold tongue

steps.action: Stated the topographic upwelling hypothesis, with the EUC deflected upward by island bathymetry (Houvenaghel 1978; Hendry & Wunsch 1973; Drazin 1961).
steps.quote: involves the encounter of a subsurface current with topography

steps.action: Took the ROGER glider estimate of vertical velocity west of the Galápagos (Jakoboski et al. 2020) and noted that it is only an average over a sampling area larger than the cold pool.
steps.quote: ROGER was only able to quantify the average upwelling velocity throughout the trapezoidal sampling area

steps.action: Posed the question of the true spatial scale and peak vertical velocity of island upwelling, and whether Argo can resolve its subsurface signature.
steps.quote: The true spatial scales of upwelling, the peak vertical velocities where upwelling is occurring

steps.action: Retrieved all Argo profiles from 2000 to 2021 in two boxes around the Gilbert and Galápagos Islands via the Argovis API and interpolated them to a 1-m grid from 5 to 500 m.
steps.quote: All Argo profiles between January 2000 and December 2021 were retrieved from two regions

steps.action: Checked the sampling density, the interannual and seasonal coverage (Figure 2), and the influence of ENSO on the 22-year means against an ENSO index (Figure S1).
steps.quote: Consideration of an ENSO index throughout the Argo era, however, suggests that 22 years of observations

steps.action: Validated the GLORYS-12v1 mean zonal circulation at 93°W against recent in situ observations before using the reanalysis (Figure S2), and noted that it does not resolve the Gilberts well.
steps.quote: a mean zonal circulation just upstream (93°W) that validates very well against recent in situ observations

steps.action: Built Argo temperature cross sections west of the Galápagos showing isotherms lifted above and depressed below, a doubled 15-20°C layer thickness, and anomalies exceeding ±1°C near 75 m confined east of 92°W (Figure 3a-b).
steps.quote: West of the Galápagos, Argo reveals a coherent local anomaly in temperature stratification that intensifies approaching the islands

steps.action: Compared the thermostad with a 1966 continuous temperature transect near Isla Isabela (Christensen 1971).
steps.quote: evidence of this thermostad approaching the Galápagos appears in a 1966 transect

steps.action: Mapped the 15-20°C layer thickness in all individual Argo profiles to confirm that the thermostad is concentrated alongside the islands (Figure S3).
steps.quote: confirms that the thermostad is indeed concentrated alongside the islands

steps.action: Found a similar subsurface temperature dipole, about half the amplitude and deeper, west of the northern and southern Gilbert Islands (Figure 4).
steps.quote: Surprisingly, Argo is also able to resolve a very similar subsurface signal just west of the much smaller Gilbert Islands

steps.action: Compared mean profiles within the upwelling zone with profiles further west using a two-sample t-test, above and below the nodal depth (Figures 3c, 4c, 4f).
steps.quote: significantly different from the mean of those further west, both above and below the nodal depth, based on a two-sample t-test

steps.action: Compared the zero-crossing depth of the anomaly dipole with the EUC core depth upstream of each archipelago (about 185 m from Johnson et al. 2002; about 80 m from ROGER).
steps.quote: the depth at which the vertically distributed temperature anomalies cross zero near the islands is also approximately the depth of the

steps.action: Judged the result consistent with the topographic upwelling hypothesis.
steps.quote: This result is consistent with the topographic upwelling hypothesis proposed for the Galápagos by Houvenaghel (1978)

steps.action: Repeated the Galápagos temperature sections with the GLORYS-12v1 reanalysis and found them consistent with Argo, while noting that GLORYS assimilates Argo (Figure 3d-e).
steps.quote: we first repeat the temperature calculations west of the Galápagos with the GLORYS-12v1 reanalysis

steps.action: Used GLORYS-12v1 zonal and vertical velocity sections to estimate the EUC approaching at about 0.4 m/s and a strong vertical divergence at its depth near the islands (Figure 3f).
steps.quote: with a strong vertical divergence of water away from the depth at which the EUC subsequently meets the islands

steps.action: Compared open-ocean and island-adjacent latitudinal sections of vertical velocity to separate topographic upwelling from wind-driven Ekman suction by magnitude and structure (Figure S4).
steps.quote: readily distinguishable from wind-driven upwelling (Ekman suction) both in magnitude and in spatial structure

steps.action: Checked the GLORYS open-ocean peak upwelling (1.7 m/day) against Johnson et al. (2001) (1.6 m/day), and contrasted it with 8.6 m/day averaged between 92°W and the Galápagos.
steps.quote: reported by Johnson et al. (2001) over the same longitude domain

steps.action: Made a crude estimate of vertical advective cooling at 50 m (about −0.5°C per day) and showed that the upwelling crosses the mixed-layer base, so it can reach SST (Figure S5).
steps.quote: A crude calculation of the magnitude of this term at 50 m

steps.action: Repeated the Argo calculations using only the strong-EUC season (April-June); the anomaly pattern was retained with higher amplitude (not shown).
steps.quote: the pattern of temperature anomalies is well-retained including their position relative to the EUC core depth

steps.action: Refined the claim: vertical divergence scales with inbound EUC velocity, and the mechanism may be general to all equatorial islands in the EUC path.
steps.quote: indicating the vertical divergence scales with the velocity of the inbound EUC

steps.action: Distinguished the mechanism from wind blocking by off-equatorial islands such as Hawaii (Xie et al. 2001), using the geometry of the surface anomalies.
steps.quote: this mechanism is readily distinguishable from those governing the impact of off-equatorial islands on the ocean circulation

steps.action: Estimated from GLORYS-12v1 that the upwelling plume occupies only 22% of the ROGER region at 50 m and locally reaches 12 m/day (Figure S6).
steps.quote: the upwelling rate within that smaller area locally reaches 12 m day

steps.action: Checked the GLORYS area-averaged vertical velocity over the ROGER region (1.2 m/day) against the independent glider estimate, resolving the paradox of low glider values.
steps.quote: which is well within the uncertainty of the glider-based estimate by Jakoboski et al. (2020)

steps.action: Acknowledged other mechanisms (wind-driven submesoscale instabilities, Forryan et al. 2021; the South Equatorial Current) as possibly complementary rather than excluded.
steps.quote: do not preclude other processes from playing a role in maintaining the cool SST

No; vertical velocity is too slow to measure, so it is inferred from Argo thermal fingerprints and reanalysis velocities
Resolve the scale, peak velocity and provenance of island upwelling with Argo
Topographic EUC deflection versus wind-driven Ekman upwelling; submesoscale wind-front processes and off-equatorial wind blocking also named
Topographic upwelling predicts an anomaly dipole crossing zero at EUC core depth, confined near the islands and larger than Ekman upwelling
Conditions found, not set: 22 years of Argo profiles and the reanalysis

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats the configuration at two contrasting archipelagos
Survives: Gilberts replication, GLORYS reproduction, strong-EUC season subset, glider area-average consistency
Topographic upwelling kept as the main mechanism, other processes not precluded

end.claim: Argo resolves a localized subsurface thermal fingerprint of vertical divergence at EUC depth within about 100 km west of both the Gilbert and Galápagos Islands, consistent with topographic upwelling by EUC blockage.

decisive_move.sentence: The 22-year Argo composite cross sections resolving the opposite-signed temperature anomalies centred on the EUC core depth next to the islands are the observation without which the claim would not exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the topographic hypothesis chose the regions and depths of Argo retrieval, but the data were collected by the Argo program independently of it. Claim: the confinement, the zero-crossing at the EUC core depth and the t-tests could have failed, but the GLORYS check is not independent (it assimilates Argo) and the Ekman exclusion is qualitative. Registration: nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Bernoulli principle and steady stratified flow past an obstacle (Drazin 1961) as the dynamical basis
Reduced-order Kalman filter data assimilation within GLORYS-12v1
Two-sample t-test and ±2 standard-error confidence intervals on mean profiles

novelty_claims.quote: we provide the first direct observations of this process occurring with consistency at two prominent archipelagos in the equatorial Pacific

limits: No review file was supplied (the acknowledgments thank E. Firing for comments during review), so no review sequence is coded. The 12 m/day peak upwelling is an estimate_with_resolution sub-claim, but no uncertainty is given; it comes from a reanalysis that assimilates Argo. The claim that the mechanism may be general to all equatorial islands is a regularity proposed from two cases, with no range tested. The strong-EUC season result is 'not shown'. The Indian and Atlantic Ocean discussion (Maldives, Knox 1974; São Tomé) is a cited synthesis, not coded as a step. The trace_series composition is used loosely: the observations are archival profiles of a persistent mean state, not traces of past events (inference). Rival exclusion of Ekman suction rests on visual comparison of sections (Figure S4) without a quantitative test. The Gilberts are analysed with Argo only, because GLORYS does not resolve them well.

disagreements.target: Jakoboski et al. (2020) ROGER glider estimate of upwelling west of the Galápagos (1-2 m/day)
disagreements.support: GLORYS shows that the upwelling plume covers only 22% of the glider sampling region and locally reaches 12 m/day, while its area average (1.2 m/day) matches the glider estimate.
disagreements.quote: This paradox is resolved by considering the area of the ROGER sampling region relative to the spatial scale of the topographic upwelling signal

disagreements.target: Forryan et al. (2021): wind-driven submesoscale instabilities drive Galápagos upwelling
disagreements.support: The topographic advective cooling centred near 30 m would cool any water entrained by wind-driven mixing, so the mechanisms are proposed as complementary.
disagreements.quote: It is possible that these various mechanisms are in fact complementary
